The Fractal Engine, Tool by Tool

A fractal designer whose controls are the mathematics drawn as a technical drawing of itself, documented the same way: every tool explained in a few lines, with the engine running underneath.

iori1

1Jorik Jonathan Chase, 3DIE — Design, Art & Technologies Label. A companion to the Fractal Engine and to paper 0. October 2026.

Open the Fractal Engine. In the engine, the page glyph at the end of the row of toggles (the menu mark, top right) brings you back here.

The paper in one paragraph

The Fractal Engine draws fractals from a formula: a short list of operations, applied to a point again and again. Everything the engine does is a reading of that repetition, the orbit. Followed forwards from every pixel it gives a cave you can fly through; followed backwards from random points it gives a nebula; fed back through itself as an image it grows the picture frame by frame. On top of the orbit sit the tools: a hold that edits whatever moves the surface under your hand, a lens that turns the view into the map of two parameters, a lineage that keeps every formula you made, a ring of neighbours to breed from, four dimensions, species mixed inside the iteration, colour and motion as networks, and collages of finished shapes. This paper takes them one at a time.

Every figure is the engine itself, set up for the tool above it. A figure starts when it scrolls into view and stops when it leaves; click or tap it to take the controls, and press outside it to give the page back its scroll. Nothing you do in a figure is saved. The line under each figure is its formula as the engine has it at that moment. The mathematics sits folded in boxes marked The mathematics. WebGPU is needed: a recent Chrome, Edge or Safari.

1. One Object: the Orbit

A formula is a list of operations. Applied to a point over and over, it gives the point's orbit, and the orbit is the only thing the engine computes.

Take a point in space, fold it into a box, fold it again through a sphere, scale it by 2.5 and add back where it started. Do it twelve times. Points near the shape stay near it; points away from it fly off. That is the Mandelbox [1], the shape you arrive in. The rule add back where it started is what makes it a Mandelbrot-type set, the same rule as z → z² + c in the plane [2].

The engine follows each orbit together with how it stretches space (its Jacobian), which branch of a fold it took, and how close it came to the origin. Colour, the surface, the glow, the chaos meter and the handles you grab are all statistics of that one trace. So the look is separate from the geometry by construction, and every tool below reads the same object.

1.1 Notation

A formula is written as one line of text. Operations are separated by a dot, numbers follow their operation, and ×12 says how many times the list runs. The arrival formula reads

fold.box 1 · fold.sphere .5 1 · scale 2.5 · +c ×12 bail=100

Twenty-nine operations make up the library: folds through a plane, a box, a box with a limit per axis, a sphere, the absolute value and a sort of the coordinates, a stepped fold (section 5.7); powers (the triplex bulb, the complex power, inversion, a twist); the affine moves (translate, +c, scale, rotate); the 4-D forms (rotate4, sort4, bulb4, quat); the lattice wrap, the Kleinian step and three seeds (section 5.6); and five flame variations for the push engine [3]. A letter word after the count is a schedule: ×12 AAB alternates two op lists, a hybrid. c=x,y,z fixes the constant and gives a Julia set; slice=…, shade=… and drive=… carry the 4-D slice, the colour network and the drivers (sections 5, 6). The line, the JSON behind it, the graph of section 5.5 and the URL are one object: every formula is its own address, and its hash is its gallery id.

The mathematics

A formula with op list f1, …, fm is the map F = fm ∘ … ∘ f1, and the orbit of a point p is p0 = p, pi+1 = F(pi), stopped after N steps or when |pi| passes the bail radius. A schedule word picks which list runs at step i. Each op carries four things: its forward map, an inverse branch (one preimage, picked at random where there are several), a rule for the running derivative, and its Jacobian. The derivative rules are few: isometries (folds, rotations, translations) leave the running scale dr unchanged, a scale multiplies it by |s|, the bulb by n rn−1, and +c adds one when c follows the point.

2. Three Ways to Draw

The same formula is drawn three ways: forwards from every pixel (pull), backwards from random points (push), and as an image fed back through its own map (loop). P or a double click cycles them.

2.1 Pull: the Cave

Pull marches a ray from the camera through every pixel. At each step it asks the formula how far the nearest surface could be, the distance estimate, and moves that far. Near the surface the steps shrink, and where they fall below a pixel the ray has hit [4] [5]. The estimate comes from the orbit itself: how far the point travelled divided by how much the formula stretched space along the way [6].

A lamp rides just off the camera, so enclosed caves are lit wherever you are; shadows and ambient occlusion appear when the view is still; depth of field focuses on whatever the centre ray hits. Every speed is the distance estimate at the camera: a hall and a crevice feel the same under the hand, and moves that would enter the surface are refused.

Two shaders draw the same formula. An interpreter reads the op list from a buffer and never recompiles, so editing is instant. A JIT writes the formula out as its own shader, every operation inlined and the loop unrolled, compiled in the background once the structure is known; it runs two to twelve times faster and takes over by itself. The two are checked against each other and against a float64 CPU reference on every change. Hover the line under a figure to see which one is drawing.

The mathematics

With r = |pN| and dr the running derivative, the engine uses two estimates. Fold formulas (an iterated function system run forwards) take

d = r / |dr|,

whether or not the orbit escaped. Power formulas take the potential-based estimate of escape-time fractals,

d = ½ · r log r / |dr| outside the set, 0 inside.

Sphere tracing is safe when d never exceeds the true distance (the estimate is a lower bound, or Lipschitz with constant 1). Operations that break the bound inside the loop, such as a rotation between folds, mark the formula not pull-safe and the march shortens its steps.

2.2 Push: the Nebula

Push runs the formula backwards. The inverse of an expanding map is a contracting one, so walking a point through random inverse branches draws the attractor, Barnsley's chaos game [7]. 32,768 walkers take 24 steps a frame; every sample lands as a small Gaussian splat whose shape follows how the inverse steps squeezed space, and the histogram is tone-mapped by log density as flames are [3]. A walk that hits a dead end backs up instead of retrying in place, so thin branches are not swallowed.

Pull and push are one formula in opposite directions. Without a fixed constant, push shows the Julia set of the point you are looking at, so one toggle gives the cave and the nebula from the same seed.

DesktopTouch
Pull → push → loopP or double clickdouble tap, or the mode glyph in the row (section 9)
The mathematics

A walker at xk takes one random preimage, xk+1 = Fj−1(xk), through the ops in reverse. The splat's covariance rides the walk,

Σ ← J Σ JT + ε² I,

with J the inverse step's Jacobian (by finite differences with the random choices replayed) and ε one pixel's footprint at the focus. The thin-lens circle of confusion is added to the projected covariance, which gives depth of field for free [8]. Brightness is the log of the density, colour the mean colour landed.

2.3 Loop: the Optical Machine

Point a camera at a monitor showing the camera's own picture and the image feeds back through the optics: the distance is a scale, the roll a rotation, the tone knobs a nonlinearity. Crutchfield showed in 1984 that this is an iterated map acting on images [9], and Dave Blair's Light Herder turned it into an instrument [10]. The loop engine is that machine with the formula as its optics: every frame, each pixel looks up where the formula sends it in the last frame, so the escape-time picture grows out of noise instead of being computed.

The screen is a window on a plane. Its knobs are the monitor's: hue rotation, saturation, gain, contrast about a dark pivot, decay, blur, a seed of sparks and how much of the field is fed in. Gain times decay just under one gives the nested halos of escape time; at or above one the set saturates.

The mathematics

One pass is

I′(y) = T( blur( I( F(y) ) ) ),

with F the formula's forward map and T the tone curve. Pulling back through F is pushing forward through its inverse branches, so the loop applies the Hutchinson operator of F's inverses to the whole image at once [12]; formulas with two op lists sum both pull-backs, the beam splitter of the optical rig. For a 3-D formula the plane shows the shadow of the dynamics.

3. Derivatives: Chaos and the Metric

Every orbit is followed together with its derivative, in position and in one parameter. From that one mechanism come the normals, the Lyapunov exponent, and a measure of how far each parameter moves the surface on screen.

The shader carries dual numbers: alongside each coordinate, how it changes when the starting point or one parameter changes [13]. Five columns ride through every orbit: three for the position gradient (the surface normal), one for the selected parameter, one for the Lyapunov exponent. The exponent says how fast nearby orbits part: negative where the dynamics is calm, positive where it is chaotic [14].

L colours the surface by it, about the view's own median: calm surfaces dark and cool, chaotic ones hot and glowing. In the Mandelbox the sphere-fold pits run hot and the box faces stay calm.

The parameter column gives the metric. A sensing pass marches a coarse grid of rays to the surface and measures, for every parameter, how many pixels the surface moves per unit. Raw sensitivities differ sixfold between the Mandelbox's parameters; divided by the metric, one pixel of hand motion moves the surface about one pixel whichever parameter it is. Every tool in section 4 is built on it.

DesktopTouch
Lyapunov channelLthe Lyapunov glyph in the row (section 9)
The mathematics

Normals are the gradient of the distance estimate from one dual orbit. The Lyapunov exponent is

λ = limn→∞ (1/n) Σi log |J(pi) vi|,   vi+1 = J vi / |J vi|,

at fixed c, along the hit point's orbit. The metric of parameter θ at a hit is the normal speed of the surface, (∂d/∂θ) / |∇d|, divided by the pixel's footprint at that depth: pixels per unit. The view's metric is the RMS over the grid's hits. GPU and CPU agree to a median gradient angle of 0.000° and a median relative ∂d/∂θ error under 6·10−5.

3.1 The Derivatives, Compiled

Nothing here is for the hand: the same pictures arrive faster. Section 2.1's JIT writes the forward orbit out as its own shader; the dual orbit that runs at every hit is compiled beside it, into the same pipeline, and the interpreter draws until it is ready. One op becomes one block: what its forward map and its derivatives share is computed once, and a branch that leaves the derivatives alone holds no code. What no hit reads (the selected parameter's column, the colour) is left out. Chimeras unroll, and drivers are written in with their derivatives. Collage pieces compile only the Lyapunov column, and a light collage loses a little: the three-piece test scene runs 3 to 5 % slower, three compiled orbits behind a switch costing about what one saves.

4. The Hand: Grab, Lens, Lineage, Breeding

There are no sliders. You edit by holding the image where you want it to change; the engine finds what moves the surface there.

4.1 Grab

Press and hold still for a moment. A sensing pass of 25 rays around the cursor ranks every parameter by how far it moves the surface there, scaled by the parameter's own size so lengths and angles compete fairly. The first is the attention op: its handle appears as its own geometry (the fold plane, the box's edges, the sphere fold's two radii, the scale as nested squares), with the reticle around the held point and the point's real orbit inside it. The ticks on the reticle's ring are the Lyapunov exponent: dense and bright where a change is about to turn chaotic. Drag sideways to edit at the metric's rate. The value appears on a dimension line; it is the only number on screen.

The mathematics

With θ0 the value at the press and m the local metric in pixels per unit, a drag of Δx pixels sets θ = θ0 + Δx / m. Parameters rank by m · max(|θ|, 0.1) (10 for angles). Pins stop the parameters that score at least a quarter of the top one at the pinned point from wandering in the drift (section 4.4).

4.2 The Atlas Lens

The Mandelbrot set is the map of the Julia sets: each of its points is a parameter, coloured by what that parameter does. The lens generalises the idea to any two parameters of any formula. Hold Shift in a grab and the view becomes the map of the attention parameter and a second one, coloured by how far (in pixels) the surface would be from the held point under each pair. The key colour sits where the surface would touch the point; a hairline marks every doubling of distance. The map spans exactly what a drag across the screen reaches. Moving travels it, both parameters change, and the field itself updates live in a round inset; letting go closes the lens and the grab carries on from there.

The mathematics

Each pixel of the lens is a pair (θ1, θ2) = (θ10 + u/m1, θ20 + v/m2), and its value is the distance estimate at the held point under that pair. The shader reads every op record through overrides that add Δθ · ∂record/∂θ, exact for parameters the record is linear in (all but rotation angles and plane normals, which the lens does not offer). It is the held point's own Mandelbrot set.

4.3 The Lineage

Every formula you make is a node in a tree: going back and editing starts a branch, so nothing is ever overwritten and yesterday's shape is always one click away, the feature the physical machine cannot have. The structure layer shows it as dots and hairlines, the big dot being now; hover a dot for its thumbnail. Moving between nodes is never a crossfade: within one structure the parameters and the camera move in 350 ms, so every frame in between is a real fractal; across structures the old image flows through the new formula's map in the loop engine. R replays the whole lineage from its root at constant visual speed. In the live engine the lineage is kept in your browser; in these figures it lives only as long as the figure.

4.4 The Breed Ring, the Archive and the Drift

Hold still for longer, 1.2 s, and eight neighbours open around the cursor. Four are near: the formula stepped 35, 60, 90 and 130 pixels across the screen in a random direction. Four come from an archive of variety that grows in the background whenever your hand is off: a MAP-Elites grid of the best formula found for each combination of how much of the view is surface and how chaotic it is [15]. They sit around the cursor in the direction of their features, and a spoke's length is how different the neighbour looks. Release on one and the field walks there at a constant visual speed; the wheel brings farther or nearer neighbours. Picking from a gallery of variations is old [16] [17]; here the distances are measured.

The drift is the same idea without the hand: when you stop, the camera glides and every unpinned parameter wanders a few pixels about its home value. Pins (F in a grab) hold the parts you want to keep; pins are how a composition is herded.

The mathematics

A neighbour D pixels away moves each unpinned parameter by θk += D zk / mk, with z a random unit vector, so its visual distance is known before it is drawn. Spoke length is 110 + 110 tanh(D/160) px. Walks move parameters linearly in time at 150 px/s by the metric. The drift is an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck walk about the home value [19], dθ = −κ(θ − θhome) dt + σ dW, with σ = 6 px/√s divided by the metric, so every parameter wanders the same few pixels on screen.

5. New Species

Three ways to mix formulas are kept apart. Breeding interpolates the parameters of one structure. A chimera blends two structures inside every iteration, a new dynamics. A collage joins finished shapes (section 7).

5.1 The Fourth Dimension

The orbit lives in four dimensions and the camera in three. A slice, an offset along w and a tilt toward it, places the 3-D world inside the 4-D one. Moving the slice is flying through the fourth dimension; tilting it turns the world toward it. A 3-D formula is a 4-D formula whose ops leave w alone, so the slice changes nothing for it until a 4-D op (rotate4, bulb4, quat, sort4) mixes w in. Quaternion Julia sets are the classic case [20].

The mathematics

The world point (x, y, z) enters the orbit as x4 = T · (x, y, z, w0), T the rotation by three tilt angles in the xw, yw and zw planes. Every layer (ops, duals, inverses, the JIT, push and loop) carries a vec4; a push sample projects back through the slice with a Gaussian weight on its distance from it.

5.2 The Chimera

Write two op lists in brackets and both run on the same point in the same iteration; the point is then blended between them. Neither formula's shape survives intact: the blend has dynamics of its own, a new species. The weight can be a constant, or a field over the point, so one species gives way to the other across a wall.

[fold.box 1 · fold.sphere .5 1 · scale 2.5 ‖ abs · sort · scale 3 · + -2 -2 0] axis .5 1.5 1 1 0 0 · +c ×12

The mathematics

p ← (1 − ω) FA(p) + ω FB(p),   ω = σ( logit w + k n̂·p + r(|p| − 1) ).

Its Jacobian is (1 − ω)JA + ωJB + (FB − FA)∇ωT. The running derivative takes Σ ωi dri, the bound on the first two terms; the field's own stretch stays out of it (it grows along escaping orbits and would destroy the estimate far from the set), so a steep wall can be overstepped a little. Push has no closed inverse: one species' inverse is a first guess, refined by Newton on the blend.

5.3 Fields and Tissue

The weight of a chimera is a field, and the field library has eight kinds: a constant, an axis, a sphere, four-dimensional noise [21], Voronoi tissue [22], and three fields read from the fractal itself, its orbit trap, its depth and its running stretch, so a formula can mix itself by its own dynamics. Tissue takes two to seven species: n cells, each one species, with soft walls between them. A field is read either at the orbit point every iteration (new dynamics) or at the world point the orbit started from (a spatial tissue: the shape varies across space).

The mathematics

Tissue weights are a softmax over the sites xj, ωj ∝ exp(−|x − xj|² / (soft · size)), site j a cell of species j mod k. A scalar field s(x) maps to k species through u = (k − 1) σ(logit w + s(x)), shared between the two species it falls between.

5.4 The Metasurface

Sixteen families (Mandelbulb, 4-D bulb, quaternion Mandelbrot and Julia, Mandelbox and its −1.5 form, Amazing Surf, Mandalay, a 4-D-rotated Mandelbox, Menger, Sierpiński, KIFS, pseudo-Kleinian with and without pillars, Apollonian, Kleinian) lie on a square as Voronoi cells, each site its family's thumbnail. Drag the crosshair and the formula follows: inside a cell the family is bred along its own two axes; across a wall, sites of one structure blend their parameters and different structures become a chimera [23]. A stroke can be played in time (a walk through the families) or laid in space (species ordered across the world along the stroke). Any formula can become a site of its own. The four lattice families of section 5.6 have no outside to frame, so their sites open with the camera inside a hall.

Site weights are πj ∝ exp(−(dj − dmin) / 0.035), so a cell is pure until about 0.1 from its wall. Sites of one structure interpolate parameters exactly; different structures join a constant-weight chimera (blend a b c …). The walls drawn are contours of max πj at 0.6, 0.8 and 0.95.

5.5 The Graph

The strip in the structure layer is a folded network. Unfolded, it is the formula drawn top to bottom: each op a glyph node, a chimera a fork into its species and a join at its field's glyph, the iteration a repeat zone with its loop up the right side and the count and schedule below. It is the formula itself, not a picture of it: every edit here is an edit of the line of text, and one node in the lineage.

5.6 Seeds: the Families That Never Escape

The formulas so far stretch space, and the distance estimate measures that stretch. A second kind only folds and inverts: at scale 1 an orbit never escapes, so there is nothing to measure and the old estimate fills all of space. These are the sphere lattices, tunnels and packings of the pseudo-Kleinian family [24], Apollonian packings [25] and Jos Leys's Kleinian limit sets [26].

They are drawn with a seed: a shape placed at the end of the iteration. An op does nothing to the point; the estimate reads the distance to the shape where the orbit ended, divided by how much the folds stretched space on the way. The fractal is the seed seen through every fold. There are three, seed.slab, seed.sphere and seed.pillar. A seed is an op like any other, so the grab, the lens, the ring and the drivers all reach its numbers. fold.cell is the box fold with a limit per axis, wrap folds space into a lattice, and kleinian is one step of Leys's algorithm, its two numbers the real and imaginary parts of the group's trace on Maskit's slice.

Change the latticegrab (4.1): cell limits, seed offset, the trace's a and bgrab

Two limits. The Apollonian slab's estimate is scaled by .4, which keeps the measured stretch under 1 at the 99th percentile, so the march stays safe. The Kleinian estimate jumps at the wrap's seam, where nearby points land on opposite sides of the lattice: the measured stretch there reaches 11 to 13 where a true distance has 1. An overstep at that seam is possible; none has been seen. In push these families read as star clusters and webs, sparse beside pull. Walking the Metasurface between two halls, a blended camera can land on a surface for a frame or two, never at rest.

The mathematics

Pseudo-Kleinian, per iteration: p ← 2·clamp(p, −l, l) − p; k = max(r²/|p|², 1); p ← k p; D ← k D. No +c. The estimate is |v(p)/D − t|, with v the distance to the seed: ½|z| for the slab, max(ρ − r, |ρz|/|p|) for the pillar. An orbit that does escape keeps r/dr. Sampled over 20,000 point pairs a half-estimate apart, the Lipschitz constant has a 99th percentile of 1.02 and a maximum of 1.9 for the slab. Kleinian: wrap into a box, turn half the box through 180° about the separation line, invert: z ← −z/|z|², shift by the trace; estimate min(y, a − y, .3)/max(dr, 2), 99th percentile 1.25.

5.7 The Mandalay Fold

DarkBeam's stepped fold, adapted by knighty [27]: where the box fold reflects each axis at one wall, fold.mandalay sorts |z| and steps the axes against each other, so faces rise into towers and domes. It stands in the Mandelbox's place in the formula, and it is what Tom Beddard's Aurullia series was built from [28].

fold.mandalay .5 .15 · fold.sphere .5 1 · scale 2.3 · rotate 0 0 10 · +c ×12

The mathematics

The estimate here is a heuristic. fold.mandalay uses the box family's r/dr and counts the fold as a stretch of 1, as Mandelbulber does. But 50.2 % of [−4, 4]³ lies on branches where one axis takes another's value: no isometry, a stretch of up to √3. Nothing has overstepped visibly. Those branches have images of no volume, so a generic point's preimages are all axis-wise, and the inverse tries those at random, checking each forward.

5.8 Subgraphs

A run of ops can be named and used in several places, so that an edit to one reaches them all. In the text it is a letter: a( … ) the first time, with its ops, and a( … ) after that with only what is its own.

fold.box 1 · a( fold.sphere .5 1 · scale ^1.8 ) · +c · rotate 0 0 15 · a( 1.4 ) ×8

The two uses are linked: the structure and every number are shared, so moving the sphere fold's radius in either moves both. A number marked with ^ is exposed: it belongs to each use, here 1.8 and 1.4, and a folded use shows it as an ordinary dimension line. Detach turns one use back into plain ops and leaves the others linked. The same link works on a piece of the shading network or the driver lane. Breeding treats a shared number as one gene that moves every use, an exposed number as one gene per use, and never touches the structure.

A definition lives in its formula, so a URL or an export carries it. To use a subgraph in another formula, the shelf keeps saved ones in this browser; placing one copies it in, with no link back.

The limits. The engine's eight slots and 64 ops count every use, because each use is real ops: a subgraph saves typing, not GPU space, and a chimera subgraph used twice takes its species' slots twice. The lens's preview of a shared number moves the first use only; the value applied on release is exact. Ramp stops can't be exposed (a ramp's map lines can). A subgraph can't contain a subgraph, and no link crosses collage pieces. A shelf holds eight entries: an entry can't be removed, and a ninth saved one pushes out the oldest.

The mathematics

A subgraph is a list laid over plain ops: { id, n, uses, expose }, the path of each use's first op and the exposed numbers. The renderer never sees it. An instanced formula packs byte for byte as its written-out form, so the shaders, duals and JITs are the same. In the metric, a shared number appears once and carries the sum of what its copies move: an upper bound, since their partials may cancel, so a step of D pixels never moves more than D.

6. Colour and Motion

Colour and motion are networks in the same graph, fed by the orbit's readings: shading nodes for colour, drivers for parameters that vary across space, along the orbit or in time.

6.1 Shading Nodes

Beside the formula's graph sits its shading frame. The orbit's readings flow out of the repeat zone into it: the fold index, the orbit trap, the depth, the Lyapunov exponent, facing, the leading species, the w axis. A colour ramp turns a number into a colour; maths nodes combine numbers (add, multiply, power, sine, bands for terraces); colour mixes combine colours; two outputs take the surface colour and the glow. The ramp has up to sixteen stops, five interpolations, three colour spaces (RGB, HSV, Oklab [29]), an input map (scale, offset, clamp, repeat, mirror, log, invert) and presets: oil, malachite, bone, prism, strata, beetle and abyss, each with the reading it suits (the orbit trap, or facing for the thin films). A new ramp starts as the colour already there, and its presets open beside it, one tap away. Colours are picked on a hue ring around a held stop: angle is hue, distance is saturation. The network is stored in the formula, so the URL, the lineage, breeding and every export reproduce the colour exactly.

The mathematics

The shading network is a typed dataflow in topological order, packed after the op records and run per hit by a small register machine (one vec4 register per node). The ramp's hue turn rotates the Oklab a, b plane after interpolation, so lightness stays put. Push splats run the same program with the readings a sample has. The GPU and the CPU evaluator agree to a median channel error of 10−7.

6.2 Drivers

A driver makes a parameter a function instead of a number. Four kinds drive: orbit readings, read every iteration (the iteration count, the radius, the trap, the running stretch, the point's coordinates), which change the dynamics; world fields read where the orbit starts (axis, sphere, noise, tissue, the start point), which vary the shape across space; time, which animates it; and other parameters, which link one op's value to another's. Maths and remap nodes sit between. A bound parameter shows its range as a band on its dimension line, with a live tick at the value the centre's orbit gives it.

A driven shape is no longer guaranteed to have a safe distance estimate, so the engine measures how steep the drivers make it and shortens the march's steps by that factor, only for driven formulas.

DesktopTouch
Add a driverhold the empty lane (inside the repeat zone) or the row above ithold

Read another parameterpull an op's line off itself into the lanethe same
Unbind, removeclick the band or the driver, Deletethree-finger tap
The mathematics

A binding sets θ = lo + v(hi − lo), with v the driver's value. Drivers whose sources are world, time or parameters are hoisted out of the loop and computed once per pixel; orbit readings run every iteration. The step factor is measured, not bounded: at every sensed hit L = |∇d| / |∇d with the drivers held|, and the march divides its steps by the 90th percentile of L, capped at 16. In the duals a driver enters the Jacobian as ∂F/∂θ · ∇θ, the same form as a chimera's field.

6.3 Drivers into Colour

The drivers are visible to the shading frame. Any driver can feed a ramp, a maths node or a mix, so one noise can bend the shape and paint it in step. Everything in colour can be bound with bands as formula parameters are: the ramp's scale, offset and hue turn, a stop's position, a maths constant, a mix's amount, and the glow's gain. A clock on the hue turns the whole ramp around the hue ring.

6.4 The Kaliset

Kali's map is a shader artist's favourite: fold by absolute value, divide by the squared length, subtract a constant, and a few iterations give dense, glittering detail [30]. The forums used it for colour and bump on other fractals. Here it is the kali node: a number computed from the point the ray hit, so any species can take it, and it feeds a ramp, a maths node or a mix like any reading. It does not change the shape.

The mathematics

p ← |p| / (p·p) − c,   from p0 = f x,

with x the hit point and n iterations. The output is the mean change of |p| from one iteration to the next, or in the other mode the least |p|.

7. Collage

A collage leaves every piece's dynamics alone and decides only where one finished surface meets the next, and what the seam looks like.

7.1 Joins

Pieces are whole formulas, up to eight, each with its own iterations, chimeras, drivers and colour. Their distance estimates are joined by smooth minima [31]: a smooth union, and the same kernels turned around for intersection and subtraction; terraced and bevelled seams, the stairs and chamfer of hg_sdf [32]; and a morph, where a field decides which piece is there. The seam width is a parameter like any other, so drivers can vary it across space. A fractal's estimate has no inside, so a cutter is given a grow: its surface pushed out by a margin, which is what a subtraction carves with.

DesktopTouch
Start a collagedrag a lineage dot onto the field, hold a Metasurface site, or carry a ring neighbour outthe collage glyph: tap a site to add it
The collage's graphGthe collage glyph
Change the joinhold the join node: ops and kernels, each drawn as its own contourhold
Seam widthdrag the dimension line under the joindrag
Add a piecethe plus left of the piecesthe plus
The mathematics

The default kernel is the quadratic smooth minimum

h = clamp(½ + ½ (b − a)/r),   d = a h + b(1 − h) − r h(1 − h),

with the cubic, exponential, circular, stairs and chamfer forms beside it. Intersection is −union(−a, −b), subtraction a ∖ b = −union(−a, b). Every union kernel's partials are non-negative and sum to one, so the join stays 1-Lipschitz when its pieces are; the chamfer's bevel is √2, and the march's step covers it. The partials also give each piece its share at a point: the readings piece and seam for the collage's own colour.

7.2 Placement and Repetition

Each piece has a rigid placement and a uniform scale, which keep its estimate exact, and may repeat: a grid with counts, a mirror, or a polar array. The repetition is measured in the piece's own units, before its size: a polar radius of 4 on a piece of size 0.25 is a ring of radius 1. Click a surface and the piece that leads there is picked; its affine frame appears in hairlines. Drag an axis to move along it, the ring to turn, the corner to scale, the centre dot to move it freely in the screen's plane. A tap on the centre dot switches the axes between the piece's own and the world's; the world frame is drawn a little dimmer. With a piece picked, its repetition cells are drawn too, the original's solid and the copies' dashed.

The mathematics

A world point reaches piece i as rep(R−1(x − t)/s), the repetition folding it into the nearest copy in the piece's own frame, so the array moves, turns and scales with the piece. Its distance is di = s · DEi(that point) − g, and the joins fold left to right: D0 = d0, Dj = joinj(Dj−1, dj). In push, each piece walks its own attractor and a sample is kept with the weight of its piece's share there, so a sample carved away by a subtraction vanishes.

8. Keeping It: Exports and State

What is on screen leaves as a 4K still, a video, a cloud of Gaussian splats or a mesh, and every file carries the formula that made it.

The still is 3840 pixels on the long side at 64 samples, rendered by the JIT in 512-pixel tiles that are each exactly their window of the full frame, so the seams do not show. The video walks the lineage from its root to here at constant visual speed, one PNG per frame. The splats are push samples captured with their covariance and written as a 3D Gaussian splatting file [33]. The mesh samples the distance estimate on a 128³ grid around the focus and extracts the surface with surface nets [34], as a binary STL.

Stills and splat files hold the whole state (formula or collage, camera, mode, look): drop one back onto the engine and it opens where it was made. The URL holds the formula too, so a link is a scene.

9. Touch and the Overlay Toggles

Desktop decides what happens; touch adapts the gesture and the layout, never the behaviour, and adds no buttons.

A phone has no keyboard, no Shift, no ⌥, no wheel and no hover. The engine answers with one rule: a second finger is the modifier, everywhere. Resting, it is Shift (the lens opens, the gizmo snaps); a quick tap is one notch of the wheel (the next op, the next knob pair, farther neighbours); a double tap pins. A touch grab aims at the crosshair in the middle of the screen, so nothing hides under the thumb. Three fingers move the 4-D slice. Two- and three-finger taps walk the lineage back and forward.

The menu mark at the top right unfolds a row of hairline glyphs, the same set on every device: the graph, shading, drivers, Metasurface, collage, structure, Lyapunov and the mode, and last a page glyph that opens this paper in a new tab. A glyph is dim while off and bright while on; every key keeps working, the row only shows them. In the live engine a second press opens the site's menu; in these figures it only folds the row.

Rest the mouse still on a node, a port, a line, a ring item or a toggle for less than half a second, or hold a finger still on it, and its name appears in small text beside it: an op by its notation (fold.box), anything else in one to three words (colour ramp, smooth union · quad, orbit trap). 10. Examples: As Published, and One Step Further

Seven fractals people know, each drawn as it was published and then taken one step further with a tool from the chapters above. Left, the original; right, the step.

The sources are the forums and programs where 3-D fractals grew up: Fractal Forums, where the Mandelbulb, the Mandelbox and the kaleidoscopic folds were posted and argued over; Fragmentarium and Mandelbulber, whose open source code holds the formulas exactly [35] [36]; and the artists who made them a medium. Each pair starts from that formula as published.

10.1 The Mandelbulb

Daniel White and Paul Nylander's power-8 bulb of 2009: in spherical coordinates, raise the radius to the eighth power and multiply both angles by eight, then add the starting point [18]. The engine's bulb 8 · +c ×10 is that formula with its derivative carried alongside (section 3). The step: a tissue in which every cell of space is a bulb of its own power, 8 or 5, with soft walls between them (section 5.3). The classic hybrids alternated whole formulas from one iteration to the next; here the species are laid out in space.

10.2 The Mandelbox at −1.5

Tom Lowe's Mandelbox, posted as the "amazing fractal" in February 2010: fold into a box, fold through a sphere, scale, add the starting point [1]. At scale −1.5 the faces turn into castles. The step is a collage (section 7): six small −1.5 boxes in a polar ring around a seventh, joined by smooth unions, a cathedral ring no single formula draws.

10.3 The Kaleidoscopic Folds

Knighty's kaleidoscopic iterated function systems of 2010: fold space across mirror planes, then stretch it about a corner [37]. The Menger sponge is abs, sort, scale 3; the Sierpiński tetrahedron three plane folds and scale 2. The step: a chimera that runs both inside every iteration and averages the point (section 5.2), a species between the sponge and the tetrahedron.

10.4 The Quaternion Julia Set

Alan Norton drew Julia sets of the quaternions in 1982; Hart, Sandin and Kauffman ray traced them with a distance estimate in 1989 [20] [5]. A three-dimensional slice of a four-dimensional set: q → q² + c. The step: drivers (section 6.2) put the constant c on a slow clock, so the slice drifts through the family of quaternion Julia sets on its own.

10.5 Amazing Surf

A Mandelbox variant from the Mandelbulber library (credited there to Kali): the box fold on two axes only, so the shape runs out into sheets and terraced "lands" [36]. It is still one of the most used formulas in Mandelbulber galleries, usually with depth of field [38]. The step: painted in one hue in terraces of the orbit trap (section 6.1), with the rotation inside its iteration on a slow clock (section 6.2), so the lands turn as you watch.

10.6 A Cave in the Manner of Fractal Nature

Julius Horsthuis's films (Foreign Nature, Recombination) made fractals into places: enveloping halls with natural light, rendered in Mandelbulb3D [39]. The engine arrives in such a hall. Painted in one hue, in terraces, with the camera's depth of field, it is the left figure. The step: the same hall with its scale changing through space, a noise driver moving it between 2.35 and 2.65 (section 6.2), so the architecture shifts as you fly through it. Enter and fly (the wheel, or a pinch). A tissue of two Mandelboxes, the obvious step, measured over half a second a frame here: too heavy for a page.

10.7 A Fractal as Gaussian Splats

3D Gaussian splatting represents a scene as millions of small coloured ellipsoids [33], and it is usually fitted to photographs. The engine makes them from the formula: push walks a Julia-type bulb backwards and every sample becomes an ellipsoid shaped by its walk (section 2.2), and the structure layer's dots glyph writes them as a file any splat viewer opens. Left, the bulb as a surface; right, the same set as splats.

11. Planned

What the engine does not do yet, in the same form as the chapters above. Nothing here runs: each section is a place held for a tool that is coming.

Two things are by design, not missing: a collage has no loop, since it has no one map to feed back through; and the real-iPhone checks (three-finger gestures, the corner marks against rounded screens) wait for a first session on the device. The design document beside the engine, fractal-engine/DESIGN.md, records every stretch, its decisions, what was measured and what was left.
